title: Sonu Nigam Showed Fans the Patch on His Shoulder and Said the Words No Singer Wants To: 'My Nerves Are Pinched.'
excerpt: The voice that raised a generation of NRIs is in pain — MRIs, CT scans, painkillers heavy enough to dull his own throat. And he is still walking onto a Mumbai stage this month anyway.
body:
There is a particular cruelty in a vocalist's body turning against the one thing the whole world loves him for. **Sonu Nigam** knows it now more intimately than he would like. On Tuesday, the man whose voice scored every diaspora wedding, every long-distance heartbreak, every Sunday afternoon of homesick Antakshari, posted a video from Mumbai that was unusually raw. No glam, no filter. Just a medical patch taped to his shoulder and a sentence that landed like a cold hand on the chest of anyone who grew up on his songs.

> "My nerves are pinched. I have been taking MRI and CT scans for a week. I have been taking a lot of medicines." — Sonu Nigam

He captioned it simply: *"13th June, Mumbai"* with a mending-heart emoji. That little punctuation mark of a heart, half-bandaged, told you everything about the mood of the thing — fragile, but not surrendering.

For the uninitiated, a pinched nerve is not a glamorous ailment. It does not photograph well. It is the slow, grinding kind of pain that radiates and refuses to be ignored, the kind that turns simple movements into negotiations. Sonu has spent the past week, by his own account, shuttling between scans and physiotherapy sessions, and he did not pretend any of it was easy. "Physiotherapy was very painful," he admitted. "I am taking painkillers now. Due to that, my throat is also a little heavy."

And there it is — the line that should make every fan flinch. The muscle relaxants doing their work on the rest of his body are also sitting heavy on the instrument itself. For a playback singer, the throat is not a body part. It is the career, the identity, the thing insurance underwriters lose sleep over. To hear **Sonu Nigam** casually note that his voice feels weighed down is to hear a Formula 1 driver mention his brakes feel a little soft. You sit up.

What is genuinely moving — and very on brand for a man who has built four decades on showing up — is that he has no intention of cancelling anything. He confirmed in the video that he is set to perform in Mumbai later this month, a concert he framed as a meaningful return to the stage after a gap. Pinched nerves, heavy throat, a week of needles and machines, and the answer is still: I'll be there.

That instinct is the whole reason the diaspora claims him as its own. Sonu Nigam is in the middle of *The Revolution*, his sprawling 30-year-celebration world tour that lights up exactly the cities where homesick Indians cluster — Wembley, San Jose, Toronto, Atlantic City, Abu Dhabi. For NRIs, a Sonu Nigam concert is not a night out; it is a pilgrimage, a chance to stand in a crowd of strangers and feel, for three hours, like the distance home has collapsed. The thought of that voice under medical strain is not abstract for them. It is personal.

There is also a quiet lesson tucked into how he handled this. He did not hide behind a publicist's statement or a vague "under the weather." He pointed the camera at the patch, named the diagnosis, and let his fans see the unglamorous reality of a body that has sung for the better part of fifty years. In an industry that airbrushes everything, that candour reads almost radical.

The medical reality deserves respect, not panic. Pinched nerves, with rest and the right treatment, very often resolve. The bigger question hanging over his fans is the one he half-answered himself: whether the heaviness in his throat is the medication talking, or something that lingers once the painkillers stop. A voice like his is not a renewable resource to be spent carelessly, and one hopes the people around him are protecting it as fiercely as his audiences would.

For now, the move is to send the man some grace — and, frankly, to take it easy on him if the Mumbai concert sounds a half-shade off his impossible standard. He is performing through pain most of us would use as an excuse to stay in bed. If you have tickets to a *Revolution* date in your city later this year, hold onto them tightly and wish the man a clean, complete recovery. The diaspora needs that voice intact for at least another thirty years. Get well soon, Sonu. The patch on the shoulder is allowed. The silence is not.
